Characteristics of a Gifted Learner

There is a difference between the bright student and the gifted learner. The bright student is a pleasure to teach and is always eager to please. He/she will most often receive many honors for academic achievements during his/her public-school experience. Gifted learners are distinct in their thinking, and no two gifted learners are exactly the same. Although it is not exhaustive, the information on pages 6-10 can help you to consider whether to consider referring your child to be screened for the Your ISD Gifted/Talented program.

Texas Education Agency Definition of Gifted/Talented

A gifted/talented student is a child or youth who performs at or shows the potential for performing at a remarkably high level of accomplishment when compared to others of the same age, experience, or environment and who

Step 1: exhibits high performance capability in an intellectual, creative, or artistic area;

Step 2: possesses an unusual capacity for leadership; or

Step 3: excels in a specific academic field. (Texas Education Code §29.121)

TEXAS TECH K-12 Gifted/Talented Program Design

The Gifted/Talented program at the elementary level is a virtual pullout program utilizing the Texas Performance Standards Project curriculum.

------------------------------------------------------------

Kindergarten-12th Grade | Identified students in these grades are served through a virtual pullout program. These students participate in an advanced thematic curriculum designed to allow for in-depth exploration of complex topics and issues that require high-level thinking. In addition to the foundational skills formally introduced, a strong emphasis is placed on further development of self-acceptance, group investigations, research skills, technology applications, leadership development and communication skills.

Students will be enrolled in an online course where a teacher will facilitate their creation and execution of projects and performances.

------------------------------------------------------------

Not Sure Which Option to Choose?

Choose 8-Week Online if you want an instructor-led university course with established dates and weekly deadlines.

Choose Self-Paced if you want an individual college course with more flexibility for you to complete your work.

Choose College Preparatory Academy if you want to enroll full time with Texas Tech K-12 and follow a structured high school-to-college pathway.

For more information about the College Prep Academy, please contact Brittany Perez at brittany.perez@ttu.edu.

TEXAS TECH K-12 Goals for Gifted/Talented Students

TEXAS TECH K-12 Gifted/Talented Students will:

Step 1: Study issues, themes, and problems of a discipline of study to create in-depth understanding

Step 2: Become creative problem-solvers and use complex thinking skills effectively

Step 3: Generate a variety of original products of professional quality through skills and information gained from in-depth study

Step 4: Develop a healthy self-concept and sense of pride in accomplishment as it relates to self and others

Step 5: Develop leadership skills that will enable these students to become leaders beyond their school days and into the work world

Referral Process

Referral of Students

During the academic school year, all students in the full-time tuition free program will have the opportunity to be referred and tested.

Teachers, administrators, and parents may refer students for the Gifted/Talented program. The referral process is held annually or as needed for students new to the district. All students referred will be screened for placement.

Purchase & Pay

Once all courses have been selected, please press "Checkout" which will take you to the Checkout process to complete course payment.

After pressing "Checkout", you should receive notification that you are being directed to Touchnet to complete payment information.

Upon entering payment information, you should receive payment confirmation.

Clicking on continue, you should receive your receipt as well as the option to print it out.

Characteristics Related to Potential Giftedness

Step 7: Student’s innovative use of common materials in the classroom or outside of it. Some students show exceptional ingenuity in using everyday materials in new ways of adapting or combining common materials to serve quite different purposes from those for which the materials were originally designed. This type of ingenuity is a good indicator of creativity and originality as well as problem-solving.

Step 8: Student’s breadth of information. There are numerous opportunities both in and out of the classroom to observe the range of topics or areas in which a student appears to have some knowledge. The breadth of information that a student has is usually a good indicator of the variety of his or her interests. It is also a good indicator of effective long-term memory and the store of information a student has, both of which are strongly related to problem-solving ability.

Step 9: Student’s depth of information in a particular area. Some students develop an extensive knowledge about some particular area such as space, birds, art, or music. A student who has gained such extensive knowledge has probably done so on his or her own as a result of an extensive long-term interest. Like breadth of information, depth of information is a good indicator of effective long-term memory and store of information, both related to problem-solving ability.

Step 10: Student’s collections of materials or hobbies. Exceptional children tend to have hobbies or to make collections of materials that are quite different from those of typical children of their age or grade group. For example, a potentially gifted fourth grade boy may have a collection of photographs of spiders’ webs, whereas other fourth grade boys collect pictures of baseball players. Sometimes the content of the collections may be the same, but the potentially gifted child organizes his or her collection in a more systematic or novel way than does the typical child. Parents are particularly good sources of information about these kinds of things.

Characteristics Related to Potential Giftedness

Step 15: Student’s preferences for complexity, difficulty, and novelty in tasks. Potentially gifted students tend to prefer to work at tasks that are complex and difficult. When permitted to choose the tasks or problems on which they work, they most frequently choose the most complex or difficult ones or ones that present new challenges to them.

Characteristics Related to Potential Giftedness

There are certain student characteristics related to potential giftedness that can be more reliably appraised by teachers, parents, and others who have extended opportunities to observe students than by tests or formal instruments. Some of the more important ones are:

Step 1: Student’s use of language. This includes such things as range of vocabulary, precision in the use of words, and complexity of sentence structure. Although these can be appraised in a test situation, one obtains a better appraisal of the level of habitual use of language through observation in a wide variety of everyday situations.

Step 2: Quality of students’ questions. Most children ask questions, and some children ask many questions. Although it is true that bright children typically ask many questions, it is the quality rather than the number of questions that discriminates most sharply between the potentially gifted child and other children. One wants to look at the unusualness of a question in relation to age or grade or the insightfulness of a question, i.e., indications that the individual has grasped the central nature of the phenomenon, or indications that the individual is relating the present task or situation to other experience.

Step 3: Quality of examples, illustrations, or elaborations that a student used in explaining something or in describing events or in telling stories. Not only do exceptional students have a good command of language, but they also tend to use examples that are apt and original or to produce unusual analogies to illustrate points. Some students show an unusual ability to translate verbal materials into pictorial modes or models or schematic diagrams. All these behaviors indicate a high level of understanding of the material that the students are using, ability to communicate ideas, and originality.

answer.text:
**Texas Tech K-12 Gifted and Talented (G/T) Program Overview**

---

**Program Design & Goals**
- The Texas Tech K-12 Gifted/Talented program is a virtual pullout program for identified students in grades K–12.
- The curriculum uses the Texas Performance Standards Project and is designed for in-depth exploration of complex topics, high-level thinking, and advanced thematic learning.
- Students participate in an online course facilitated by a teacher, focusing on projects and performances.
- Emphasis is placed on self-acceptance, group investigations, research skills, technology, leadership, and communication.

**Goals for Gifted/Talented Students**
- Study issues, themes, and problems of a discipline for in-depth understanding.
- Become creative problem-solvers and use complex thinking skills.
- Generate original, professional-quality products through in-depth study.
- Develop a healthy self-concept and pride in accomplishment.
- Develop leadership skills for future success.

---

**Texas Education Agency Definition of Gifted/Talented**
A gifted/talented student is a child or youth who:
- Performs at or shows potential for performing at a remarkably high level of accomplishment compared to others of the same age, experience, or environment.
- Exhibits high performance capability in intellectual, creative, or artistic areas.
- Possesses an unusual capacity for leadership.
- Excels in a specific academic field. (Texas Education Code §29.121)

---

**Referral Process**
- Teachers, administrators, and parents may refer students for the G/T program.
- The referral window is the last two weeks of January each year.
- All referred students are screened for placement.
- The process is annual or as needed for new students.

---

**Characteristics of Gifted Learners**
- Asks many and high-quality questions.
- Highly curious and mentally/physically involved.
- Shows advanced conceptualization and abstract thinking.
- Demonstrates unusual memory and interest in various topics.
- Shows independence, persistence, and a drive for perfection.
- Exhibits leadership, humor, and creativity.
- Uses advanced language, quantitative reasoning, and problem-solving strategies.
- Has broad and/or deep knowledge in specific areas.
- Prefers complexity, novelty, and challenging tasks.

---

**Distinguishing Gifted Learners from Bright Students**
- Gifted learners often ask more questions, are more curious, and thrive on complexity.
- They may prefer adults, construct abstractions, and initiate projects.
- They are highly self-critical and enjoy learning for its own sake.

---

**Contact Information**
- Administration Office Contacts:
  - Braxton Allison, Principal, Texas Tech K-12
  - Cari Moye, Principal: Recruitment, Investment, Strategic Partnerships & Pathways and Engagement (RISE)
  - Paige Barnes, Director of Special Populations
  - Keetha Chadwick, Director of Assessment and Accountability
  - Charlotte Ward, Counselor
  - Melissa Francis, Teacher

---

**Additional Notes**
- The program is designed to serve the unique needs of gifted learners through advanced curriculum and enrichment opportunities.
- For more information or to refer a student, contact the Texas Tech K-12 administration.

**Gifted and Talented (G/T) Information for Parents — Texas Tech K-12**

---

**Program Overview**
- The Texas Tech K-12 Gifted/Talented program is a virtual pullout program for identified students in grades K–12.
- Students participate in an advanced, thematic curriculum designed for in-depth exploration, high-level thinking, and creative problem-solving.
- The program uses the Texas Performance Standards Project curriculum and is facilitated online by a teacher.

---

**Goals for Gifted/Talented Students**
- Study complex issues and themes for deeper understanding.
- Develop creative problem-solving and complex thinking skills.
- Produce original, high-quality work through in-depth study.
- Build leadership skills and a healthy self-concept.

---

**Referral and Identification Process**
- Students can be referred by teachers, administrators, or parents.
- The referral window is the last two weeks of January each year.
- All referred students are screened for placement in the program.

---

**Characteristics of Gifted Learners**
Parents should look for the following traits:
- Asks many and high-quality questions; highly curious.
- Advanced language use and abstract thinking.
- Strong memory, deep interest in topics, and persistence.
- Shows leadership, creativity, and a sense of humor.
- Prefers complex, challenging tasks and may prefer adult company.

**Bright Child vs. Gifted Learner**
- Bright children know the answers and work hard; gifted learners ask questions, are highly curious, and may show more independence and creativity.

---

**Program Structure**
- Identified students join an online course with a teacher who guides projects and performances.
- Emphasis on research, technology, leadership, and communication skills.
- The program is designed to foster both academic and personal growth.

---

**Contact Information**
For questions or to refer your child:
- Braxton Allison, Principal, Texas Tech K-12
- Paige Barnes, Director of Special Populations
- Charlotte Ward, Counselor

---

**Next Steps for Parents**
- If you believe your child may be gifted, consider referring them during the annual referral window.
- Contact the Texas Tech K-12 administration for more details or support.

**Texas Tech K-12 District Partnership Program — Information for Parents**

---

**Overview**
- Texas Tech K-12 partners with school districts to provide students access to online courses and Credit by Exams (CBEs).
- District Partnership students use the Focus Student Portal to access their courses, grades, and communicate with teachers.

---

**Key Features for Parents**
- **Flexible Online Learning:** Students can take courses not offered at their local school, recover credits, or accelerate their learning.
- **Progress Monitoring:** Parents and students can view course progress, grades, and schedules through the Focus Portal.
- **Communication:** Students can communicate directly with Texas Tech K-12 teachers through the portal.
- **Support:** Texas Tech K-12 provides technical and academic support for district partnership students.

---

**Parent Involvement**
- Parents can help students stay on track by monitoring progress in the Focus Portal and encouraging regular course engagement.
- For questions or support, parents can contact the Texas Tech K-12 Support Team at 1-800-692-6877 or submit a support ticket.

---

**Technology Requirements**
- Students need a modern computer (≤5 years old), reliable internet, and a unique email address.
- Recommended browsers: Google Chrome (required for online exams), Firefox, Edge, or Safari.
- Mobile devices (phones, tablets, Chromebooks) should not be used as the primary device for coursework or proctored exams.

---

**Accessing the Focus Portal**
- Students log in to the Focus Portal to view their courses, grades, and communicate with teachers.
- The portal link: [Focus Portal](https://ttu.focusschoolsoftware.com/focus/index.php)

---

**Support Contacts**
- For technical or academic support: 1-800-692-6877

Address account or technology issues as soon as possible. Waiting until an assignment is due can create unnecessary problems, and technical difficulties do not automatically extend course deadlines.

Students with Disabilities

Online instruction presents different challenges than those in a traditional classroom. The curriculum is rigorous and is reading- and writing-intensive. Successful online students are able to take initiative and manage their own time.

Nevertheless, Texas Tech K-12 strives to offer exceptional education programs that meet the needs of students with disabilities. To qualify, the student's Individual Education Plan (IEP) needs to indicate that the Texas Tech K-12 online program is the appropriate instructional setting for the student and is the student’s least restrictive environment.

The student’s admission, review, and dismissal (ARD) committee has the responsibility of determining whether or not an electronic (online) course/program will meet the needs of a student with a disability. The committee will also take into account the nature of the asynchronous program and what services can be implemented online. It is crucial to note that the program is fully online, providing only services that can be provided virtually as the school does not have a physical location. The ARD committee will make an informed decision about an online program and the educational appropriateness of this academic setting for a student and his or her particular academic needs.
